the acquirer is not accountable for the obligations of the insolvent company, except for the obligations that are expressly transferred to it by the insolvency proceedings, and for which it has been declared accountable.
the acquirer is responsible for all the obligations of the insolvent company, except for those arising from employment contracts and Social Security contributions.

, in the context of an insolvent procedure, the transmission of a business or an operating unit by the insolvent debtor, may give rise to a number of legal questions, particularly from the labour and social security perspective, in relation to the acquirer's responsibility.
In summary, our research is concerned with

determining whether or not the acquirer is liable, and the extent of such liability, when the insolvent company transfers a company or operating unit to the acquirer in the context of an insolvent company's liquidation.

the following questions: 1) Is the acquirer of the insolvent company or operating unit responsible for the debts of the insolvent debtor in the insolvency phase? 2) If there is responsibility, what is the nature of that responsibility? 3) What is the scope of the responsibility?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the acquirer is not liable for the liabilities of the insolvent company, unless the acquirer has acted in bad faith.

, in the absence of an express provision, the acquirer is liable for the debts of the insolvent company in the same terms as the insolvent company, with the exception of those that are expressly excluded from transmission, such as the social security debts.

the acquirer is accountable for the labour and Social Security debts of the insolvent company in the liquidation phase of the insolvency procedure, provided that the acquirer has been able to verify the existence of the debt.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the case of a transmission of an operating unit by a company in the process of bankruptcy, the acquirer is accountable for the debts that were incurred by the insolvent business prior to the transmission, provided that the transmission is carried out in the context of an ongoing bankruptcy process.

, as a general rule, the acquirer of a company or operating unit is not accountable to the workers and pensioners of the insolvent company for the obligations arising from the employment relationship or from the Social Security contributions.
the current legislation does not provide a clear solution to the issue of liability of the acquirer of the company in the liquidation phase.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is no consensus on this issue, which is why it is important to continue working to clarify the matter and provide a solution that is in the interests of the parties involved and the economy as a whole.

, although the current legislation does not expressly provide a solution to the issue of the liability of the acquirer of an insolvent company's assets in labour and Social Security matters, there is a clear tendency to consider the acquirer liable in the same way as the seller, in the same terms as the insolvency proceedings would have had the insolvent company continued to exist.

, in the absence of any specific regulation on the matter, it seems that the acquirer's responsibility will be governed by the general rules on transfer of assets and liabilities in the event of a merger, and that the acquirer will be responsible for any debts that the insolvent company may have incurred prior to the transfer of the company or operating unit.
